title: Диверсия во имя «Спартака»  (Sabotage in the Name of Spartak)

segments.t: Furious that Vika confused Zenit's goalkeeper Malafeev with a Spartak player, Chef Barinov consults his fish Arkasha and decides fate has handed him a chance to help his team win tomorrow. Ignoring Lyova's protests that poisoning a guest is dishonorable, Barinov spikes a complimentary dish with expired ingredients.
И что же мне делать, Аркаша?
Другого такого шанса может не быть.
Alright, let's go through it step by step in English.
И что же мне делать, Аркаша?
'So what am I supposed to do, Arkasha?' Barinov probes openly in the scene, joining "delat" ("do") to "chto" ("what") so every word pulls its weight.
'Zenit has to lose.' Lyova favors an honest note as they talk, combining "dolzhen" ("has to, must") and "proigrat" ("lose") so the key meaning lands right away.
Другого такого шанса может не быть.
'There might never be another chance like this.' Barinov maintains a wry view at once, pairing "drugogo" ("other, another") with "shansa" ("chance") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
'We have to help Spartak.' Lyova picks a natural tack in this beat, weaving "nado" ("it is necessary") together with "pomoch" ("to help") just the way native speakers do.
'And what do you think?' Barinov probes quietly toward Lyova here, putting "dumayesh" ("think") alongside "ty" ("you") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'I agree with him.' Lyova shares an honest position on the spot, putting "soglasen" ("agreed") alongside "ya" ("I") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Take it away from him.' Barinov shows a resolute line toward Lyova, building the phrase around "otorvali" ("to tear off") and "yego" ("him") for a crisp, natural delivery.
'Chef, there is a complimentary dish from the chef.' Lyova conveys a steady attitude in the conversation, anchoring the Russian line on "tam" ("there") and "blyudo" ("dish") without extra filler.
'Chef, what are you doing?' Lyova inquires promptly as the beat lands, putting "delayete" ("are doing") alongside "shef" ("Chef") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Lyova, go away.' Lyova keeps an earnest tack at once, putting "idi" ("go") alongside "lev" ("Lev") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'I will handle this myself.' Barinov favors a direct note in their talk, pairing "razberus" ("I will sort out") with "ya" ("I") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
'That is underhanded, Chef.' Lyova favors an earnest course in front of Barinov, using "podlo" (from "podat", "to submit, file") alongside "eto" ("this") to shape the meaning.
'I said go.' Barinov conveys a measured position without hesitation, building the phrase around "skazal" ("said") and "ya" ("I") for a crisp, natural delivery.
И что же мне делать, Аркаша?
Другого такого шанса может не быть.
That wraps up this scene as chef Barinov decides he must help his beloved club by giving Zenit's goalkeeper mild food poisoning before tomorrow's match, ignoring Lyova's protests. Until next time!
